title: A finite birational map to a nodal curve with connected fibres is an isomorphism
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field] [def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $X$ and $Y$ be reduced [def-pc-reduced-scheme] finite-type $k$-schemes [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], pure of dimension one [def-weil-pure-dimension]. Assume $Y$ is nodal: every nonsmooth closed point [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] has completed local ring [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion] isomorphic as a $k$-algebra to $k[[u,v]]/(uv)$ [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series]. Let $f:X\to Y$ be finite and surjective [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism]. Suppose there is an open $U\subset Y$ meeting every irreducible component [def-weil-irreducible-components] such that $f^{-1}(U)\to U$ is an isomorphism, and that every geometric fibre [def-weil-geometric-fibre] of $f$ is connected [def-weil-connected-scheme]. Then $f$ is an isomorphism. Neither $X$ nor $Y$ is required to be connected, separated or proper over $k$.

source.place: Appendix B, ordinary-point characterization by absence of nontrivial bijective finite modifications, printed p. 57, and normalization description on printed pp. 56--57; nodal special case, stated locally on the target; primary text read online, local archival copy WANTED

proof.text: Because $X$ and $Y$ are finite type over the field $k$, they are Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian], and hence have finitely many irreducible components by [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-finitely-many-components]. Every fibre of $f$ is finite: over an affine open $\operatorname{Spec}R\subseteq Y$ the finite morphism is $\operatorname{Spec}A\to\operatorname{Spec}R$ with $A$ a finite $R$-module, so the fibre over $y$ is the spectrum of the finite-dimensional $\kappa(y)$-algebra $A\otimes_R\kappa(y)$, which has finitely many prime ideals. Let $Z$ be an irreducible component of $X$ with generic point $\xi$. If $f(\xi)$ were a closed point $y$, then by continuity $Z=\overline{\{\xi\}}\subseteq f^{-1}(y)$ would be finite, contradicting $\dim Z=1$. So $f(\xi)$ is a non-closed point of the one-dimensional scheme $Y$; its closure is irreducible of dimension one, hence an irreducible component of $Y$, and $f(\xi)$ is its generic point. The open $U$ meets every component, so it contains every generic point of $Y$; thus every generic point of $X$ lies in $f^{-1}(U)$. The isomorphism $f^{-1}(U)\simeq U$ therefore identifies the generic points of $X$ and $Y$ bijectively, component by component, with isomorphic local rings there; no two source components map to the same target component, and each target component is the image of exactly one source component. Restricting $f$ to corresponding reduced components gives a finite dominant morphism inducing an isomorphism of their function fields.

source.place: Tag 01T6, finite type over a Noetherian base; Properties Tag 0BA8, finitely many irreducible components; generic-point argument for the dense open.

proof.text:
Let $
u:\widetilde Y	o Y$ be the disjoint union of the normalizations of the reduced irreducible components of $Y$. The map $\mathcal O_Y	o f_*\mathcal O_X$ is injective: a local section $s$ of $\mathcal O_Y$ killed by it vanishes on the dense open $U$, so the closed set where its germ lies in the maximal ideal is everything, $s$ is locally nilpotent, and $s=0$ because $Y$ is reduced. As $X$ is reduced, $f_*\mathcal O_X$ embeds in the product of the pushforwards of the structure sheaves of its components. On a corresponding pair of components (Step 1), the finite ring map is integral by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-algebra-is-integral] and has the same function field. By the definition [def-sc-normalization], its image lies in the integral closure, so componentwise the structure sheaves fit into inclusions $\mathcal O_Y\subseteq f_*\mathcal O_X\subseteq
u_*\mathcal O_{\widetilde Y}$. The normalization properties [lem-sc-normalization-properties] identify $
u$ as finite and birational and make it an isomorphism over the normal locus. Let $y$ be a smooth point of $Y$; its local ring is regular, hence a domain, so $y$ lies on exactly one component $Y_i$. Choose an affine open $V
i y$ inside the smooth locus that misses every other component; then $V$ is integral, and it is a smooth curve over $k$ in the sense of [lem-sc-smooth-normal], so every local ring of $V$ is normal. By Step 1, $f^{-1}(V)$ is an open subset of the single corresponding component of $X$, hence integral, and $f^{-1}(V)	o V$ is finite and maps generic point to generic point with an isomorphism of local rings there. By [lem-trf-finite-birational-normal-iso] it is an isomorphism. Thus the quotient between the first and second sheaves is supported only at the nodal points.

source.place: Tag 0AB1, finite birational map over a normal target; Tag 035Q, normalization; nodal-curve smooth-locus argument.

proof.text: Fix a nodal point $y\in Y$. For the normalization in Step 2 write $B=(\nu_*\mathcal O_{\widetilde Y})_y$ and write $R=\mathcal O_{Y,y}$ and $A=(f_*\mathcal O_X)_y$. The ordinary-point statement [lem-trf-ordinary-point-delta-branches] applies to $Y$ and says that a node has two normalization branches and $\dim_k(B/R)=1$. Since $R\subseteq A\subseteq B$ are $k$-algebras, $A/R$ is a $k$-linear subspace of the one-dimensional $k$-vector space $B/R$. Hence either $A=R$ or $A=B$.

source.place: Appendix B, ordinary n-fold point characterization preceding Lemma B.1, printed pp. 56--57; local stalk quotient.

proof.text: The case $A=B$ is impossible. Indeed, after tensoring with the residue field $k$ at $y$, the fibre algebra of $f$ is then the same as the fibre algebra of the normalization $\nu$. The two normalization branches from Step 3 give two distinct points in this finite fibre; a finite $k$-scheme with two distinct points is a disjoint union of its two local factors and is disconnected. Since $k$ is algebraically closed, this is already the geometric fibre, contradicting the hypothesis that every geometric fibre of $f$ is connected. Therefore $A=R$ at every node.

source.place: Finite affine fibres and the two-branch normalization at an ordinary node; connectedness definition.

proof.text: Step 2 gives equality of $\mathcal O_Y$ and $f_*\mathcal O_X$ on the smooth locus, and Step 4 gives equality at every node. Thus the natural map $\mathcal O_Y\to f_*\mathcal O_X$ is an isomorphism on all stalks. A finite morphism is affine on affine opens, so equality of these structure sheaves makes the induced affine ring maps isomorphisms on an affine cover of $Y$; consequently $f$ is an isomorphism.

source.place: Tag 0AB1, final affine-local conclusion; finite morphisms are affine.
